content: 1. The panel strongly believes that the existence of an Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) program is a fundamental requirement for any IPC-related actions to be effective. 2. Section 1a of the guidelines is closely connected to section 1b, offering a comprehensive statement of good practices and detailed information on organizing a national IPC program. 3. National IPC programs and healthcare facility-level IPC programs should be interconnected and work synergistically to achieve optimal outcomes. 4. IPC programs must have clearly defined objectives tailored to local epidemiology and priorities, based on risk assessments. These objectives should align with efforts to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) within healthcare settings. 5. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified that IPC programs should include specific activities, such as: Surveillance of HAIs and AMR. IPC measures to ensure the safety of patients, visitors, and healthcare workers, while preventing AMR transmission. Development or adaptation of guidelines and standard operating procedures for effective preventive practices, along with their implementation. Outbreak prevention and response, including triage, screening, and risk assessment, particularly during community outbreaks of communicable diseases. Education and practical training for healthcare workers. Maintenance of effective aseptic techniques in healthcare practices. Assessment and feedback on compliance with IPC practices. Ensuring continuous procurement of adequate IPC supplies, including innovative equipment when necessary, and functioning water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services. Guaranteeing that patient care activities occur in a clean and hygienic environment supported by appropriate infrastructure. 6. The GDG emphasized the importance of having dedicated, trained IPC professionals in every acute care facility. A minimum ratio of one full-time infection preventionist (nurse or physician) per 250 hospital beds is recommended, though a higher ratio (e.g., one per 100 beds) may be necessary due to increasing patient acuity and complexity. 7. All infection preventionists should undergo regular reviews and updates of their infection control competencies to ensure they remain effective in their roles. 8. While the evidence review primarily focused on acute care facilities, the GDG stressed the importance of IPC support across all types of healthcare facilities. This support could include IPC committees, trained teams serving multiple facilities, and infection preventionists conducting regular visits to outpatient and peripheral facilities. 9. Clinics providing specialized care for patients with highly transmissible diseases (e.g., tuberculosis) should have an IPC program or on-site service to prevent disease spread. 10. Reporting lines for IPC teams should be clearly defined both within healthcare facilities and externally, ensuring alignment with national programs and public health initiatives. 11. Efficient communication mechanisms should be established between facilities, authorities, and public health services to facilitate the reporting of communicable diseases and AMR-related events. 12. Data management systems are essential to support IPC activities and should be prioritized. 13. IPC programs are a critical component of safe, high-quality healthcare delivery. HAIs are among the most common complications affecting patients and healthcare workers, leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs, as well as contributing to AMR. 14. A 2011 WHO report indicated that 7% of patients in developed countries and 10% in developing countries acquire at least one HAI at any given time. A 2015 WHO survey revealed significant gaps in IPC capacity globally, with only 41% of countries having a national IPC program and even fewer extending these programs to all tertiary hospitals. 15. The GDG reviewed evidence on the effectiveness of IPC programs in reducing HAIs and AMR. For example, a landmark study by Haley et al. demonstrated significant reductions in urinary tract infections, post-surgical pneumonia, and bacteremia among high-risk patients following the implementation of an IPC program. 16. However, the evidence base is limited, with studies primarily conducted in high-income countries and some dating back over 30 years. This highlights the need for updated research reflecting the current complexity of healthcare and IPC roles. 17. The GDG recommends a ratio of one infection preventionist per 100 hospital beds, but no less than one per 250 beds, based on available evidence and the evolving demands of healthcare settings. 18. There is a need for additional research, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), to evaluate the effectiveness, cost-efficiency, and optimal composition of IPC programs. 19. The GDG unanimously agreed that nursing staff should play a central role in IPC programs, especially in LMICs where healthcare is often nurse-driven. If resources allow, IPC programs should include both doctors and nurses with specialized IPC training, as well as trained cleaning and janitorial staff. 20. Facility leadership must support IPC programs by providing materials, organizational backing, and a dedicated budget. This budget should also ensure the proper functioning of WASH services necessary for IPC activities. 21. IPC teams should establish strong links and communication mechanisms with key services, including laboratories, waste management, sanitation, water supply, cleaning, sterilization, occupational health, pharmacy, and patient safety. 22. The GDG emphasized the importance of collaboration between IPC teams and occupational health professionals to address healthcare worker safety, including post-exposure prophylaxis, outbreak management, and the selection of optimal personal protective equipment. 23. High-quality microbiological laboratory support is critical for the success of IPC programs.
